short: Guarantees that if a transaction reads a row, it will see the same data if it reads that row again later in the same transaction — preventing both dirty reads and non-repeatable reads — typically by holding read locks or using MVCC snapshot
answer: Guarantees that if a transaction reads a row, it will see the same data if it reads that row again later in the same transaction — preventing both dirty reads and non-repeatable reads — typically by holding read locks or using MVCC snapshots, though phantom reads may still be possible depending on the database.
interview: Guarantees that if a transaction reads a row, it will see the same data if it reads that row again later in the same transaction — preventing both dirty reads and non-repeatable reads — typically by holding read locks or using MVCC snapshots, though phantom reads may still be possible depending on the database.

title: Explain `SERIALIZABLE`.
short: The strictest isolation level — transactions are guaranteed to behave as if executed one at a time in some serial order, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads entirely, at the cost of the heaviest locking/contentio
answer: The strictest isolation level — transactions are guaranteed to behave as if executed one at a time in some serial order, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads entirely, at the cost of the heaviest locking/contention and highest chance of transactions being aborted and retried.
interview: The strictest isolation level — transactions are guaranteed to behave as if executed one at a time in some serial order, preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads entirely, at the cost of the heaviest locking/contention and highest chance of transactions being aborted and retried.

title: What is a composite index and how does column order matter?
short: A composite index covers multiple columns, and the leading column order affects which predicates and sort operations can use it efficiently.
answer: For an index on (customer_id, created_at), queries filtering by customer_id can use the leading portion efficiently. A query filtering only by created_at may not benefit in the same way.
code:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created
ON orders(customer_id, created_at);
followups: How would you choose index column order?
Can an index help ORDER BY?
mistakes: Adding every column to an index.
Ignoring write and storage costs.
interview: Composite index design follows actual query patterns. I consider equality predicates, range predicates, ordering and selectivity, not just individual column popularity.

title: What is a covering index?
short: A covering index contains all columns needed by a query, allowing the database to answer it from the index without fetching table rows in some engines.
answer: Whether an index is covering depends on the database and query plan. It can reduce random table access but increases index size and write cost.
followups: How do you verify a covering index is used?
mistakes: Assuming every index lookup avoids table access.
Over-indexing large tables.
interview: A covering index can satisfy a query from index data alone when the optimizer chooses it. I verify the actual execution plan.

title: What is a window function?
short: A window function computes a value across related rows without collapsing them into one row per group.
answer: Functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, SUM and LAG can calculate per-row analytics while retaining row detail.
mistakes: Using GROUP BY when row-level detail is required.
Confusing RANK gaps with DENSE_RANK.
interview: Window functions let me calculate rankings, running totals and comparisons while preserving individual rows.

title: What is a CTE?
short: A common table expression gives a query a named intermediate result, improving readability and enabling recursive queries where supported.
answer: WITH creates a logical query block. It can simplify multi-step transformations and recursive hierarchy traversal. Whether it is materialized or inlined depends on the database and optimizer.
followups: When would a recursive CTE be useful?
mistakes: Assuming every CTE is materialized.
Using CTEs without checking the plan for performance-critical queries.
interview: CTEs make complex SQL easier to structure and can express recursion. I still inspect the execution plan for important queries.

title: Explain EXPLAIN and execution plans.
short: An execution plan shows how the database intends to execute a query, such as scans, joins, sorts and index usage.
answer: EXPLAIN helps identify full scans, poor join order, large row estimates, expensive sorts and missing indexes. EXPLAIN ANALYZE, where supported, compares the plan with actual execution behavior.
code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
followups: Why can an index still be ignored?
mistakes: Optimizing from SQL text alone.
Assuming an index is always faster.
interview: I use the execution plan to understand where database time and row processing occur. I compare estimates with actuals when the database supports it.

title: What causes a database deadlock?
short: A deadlock occurs when transactions hold resources while waiting for resources held by each other, creating a cycle.
answer: A common pattern is transaction A locking row 1 then waiting for row 2 while transaction B locks row 2 then waits for row 1. Databases detect cycles and abort one transaction.
code:
T1: lock(A) -> wait(B)
T2: lock(B) -> wait(A)
followups: Why must applications retry some deadlock failures?
mistakes: Saying deadlocks mean the database is broken.
Retrying without making the transaction safe to repeat.
interview: Deadlocks are cyclic resource waits. I reduce them through consistent lock ordering, short transactions and appropriate indexing, and I handle transient deadlock failures with bounded retries when safe.

title: What is database normalization?
short: Normalization structures data to reduce unnecessary duplication and update anomalies.
answer: First, second and third normal forms progressively constrain dependencies and repeating groups. Practical systems sometimes denormalize intentionally for read performance, but the trade-off should be explicit.
code:
Customer(id, name)
Order(id, customer_id, total)
-- customer data is not repeated in every order row
mistakes: Treating normalization as a performance rule.
Denormalizing without a consistency strategy.
interview: Normalization improves integrity by reducing redundancy. I denormalize only when a measured access pattern justifies the additional consistency cost.

title: What is keyset pagination?
short: Keyset pagination uses a stable ordered key as the cursor instead of skipping a large number of rows with OFFSET.
answer: For large datasets, WHERE created_at < :lastCreatedAt ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 can avoid scanning and discarding many preceding rows. The ordering must be deterministic, often using a unique tie-breaker.
code:
SELECT id, created_at, total
FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < (:createdAt, :id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;
followups: How do you handle duplicate timestamps?
mistakes: Using only a non-unique timestamp as the cursor.
Assuming keyset is convenient for arbitrary page jumps.
interview: Keyset pagination is efficient for deep scrolling because the database seeks from a cursor rather than skipping large offsets.

title: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
short: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE removes table data in a database-specific bulk operation, and DROP removes the table object itself.
answer: DELETE can filter rows and typically generates row-level changes. TRUNCATE is generally faster for clearing a table but has database-specific transactional and identity behavior. DROP removes the schema object.
followups: Which operations can be rolled back?
How does TRUNCATE affect identity values in your database?
mistakes: Giving database-independent rollback claims.
Using TRUNCATE when row-level filtering is required.
interview: DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP have different scope and transactional semantics. For interviews I state that exact behavior depends on the database engine.

title: How do isolation levels affect concurrency?
short: Isolation levels define which concurrent transaction effects can be observed, trading consistency guarantees against concurrency and locking behavior.
answer: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but can allow non-repeatable reads. REPEATABLE READ provides stronger repeatability, while SERIALIZABLE provides the strongest standard isolation at a higher concurrency cost. Exact implementation varies by database.
code: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
followups: Dirty vs non-repeatable vs phantom read?
mistakes: Claiming isolation levels behave identically across databases.
Ignoring the cost of stronger isolation.
interview: Isolation is a concurrency contract. I choose the weakest level that satisfies business correctness, then validate the database-specific behavior and performance.

title: How would you find duplicate records?
short: GROUP BY with HAVING identifies duplicate key combinations; a window function can also mark individual duplicate rows.
answer: For duplicate emails, GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 identifies duplicated values. ROW_NUMBER can then select which rows to retain or remove.
code:
SELECT email, COUNT(*)
FROM student
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
followups: How would you delete duplicates while keeping one row?
How do you prevent duplicates after cleanup?
mistakes: Grouping by unrelated columns.
Cleaning duplicates without adding a unique constraint afterward.
interview: I first identify duplicate business keys with GROUP BY/HAVING, then use a deterministic rule to retain one row and add a constraint if uniqueness is required.

title: How does a composite index work?
short: A composite index indexes multiple columns in a defined order, and that order affects which predicates can efficiently use the index.
answer: For an index on (customer_id, status, created_at), queries filtering by customer_id are well supported, while a query filtering only by created_at may not benefit as much.
code: CREATE INDEX idx ON orders(customer_id, status, created_at);
followups: How do equality and range predicates affect column order?
mistakes: Choosing columns randomly in a composite index.
interview: Column order matters. I design composite indexes from actual query predicates and sort requirements, not just from the list of columns in a table.

title: How do you read an SQL execution plan?
short: An execution plan shows how the optimizer intends to access tables, join rows and apply filters.
answer: I look for full scans on large tables, unexpected join algorithms, poor row estimates, expensive sorts, repeated lookups and whether predicates use useful indexes. Then I compare estimated and actual behavior when available.
code: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;
followups: Why can an index still be ignored?
mistakes: Optimizing from SQL text without checking the plan.
interview: I use the execution plan to identify the actual expensive operations and verify whether indexes, join order and row estimates match the workload.

title: What is a window function in SQL?
short: A window function calculates a value across related rows without collapsing them into one row per group.
answer: Functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, SUM and LAG can calculate rankings, running totals and previous-row comparisons while preserving detail rows.
code: SELECT employee_id, salary, RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employee;
mistakes: Using GROUP BY when row-level detail must be preserved.
interview: Window functions calculate across a defined window while retaining individual rows, making them ideal for ranking and running calculations.

title: What is the difference between RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER?
short: ROW_NUMBER assigns unique sequential numbers; RANK leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK does not leave gaps.
answer: For salaries 100, 100, 90, ROW_NUMBER gives 1,2,3; RANK gives 1,1,3; DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2.
code: SELECT salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC), RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC), DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employee;
followups: Which should you use for top 3 distinct salaries?
mistakes: Saying RANK and DENSE_RANK behave identically.
interview: ROW_NUMBER is unique per row, RANK preserves tie positions with gaps, and DENSE_RANK preserves ties without gaps.

title: How do you find the top N records per group?
short: Use a window ranking function partitioned by the grouping key and filter the rank in an outer query.
answer: For top three salaries per department, calculate ROW_NUMBER or DENSE_RANK over each department ordered by salary, then filter the result.
code: SELECT * FROM (SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) rn FROM employee e) x WHERE rn <= 3;
followups: How do you handle departments with fewer than N rows?
mistakes: Using a global LIMIT N.
interview: Partition the ranking by the group and filter the rank in an outer query. This gives N rows or N distinct ranks per group depending on the chosen function.

title: What is a CTE and when would you use one?
short: A common table expression gives a named query expression that can simplify complex SQL.
answer: CTEs improve readability, can support recursive queries and can make multi-step transformations easier to reason about. Whether they materialize depends on the database and query plan.
code: WITH high_value AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 1000) SELECT * FROM high_value;
followups: When can a CTE hurt performance?
mistakes: Assuming every CTE is materialized.
interview: A CTE is primarily a query-organization tool and can support recursion. I still inspect the execution plan rather than assuming a performance benefit.

title: What is a recursive CTE?
short: A recursive CTE repeatedly evaluates a query to traverse hierarchical or graph-like data.
answer: It has an anchor query and a recursive query joined by UNION ALL. It is useful for employee hierarchies, category trees and dependency chains.
code: WITH RECURSIVE org AS (SELECT id, manager_id FROM employee WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.manager_id FROM employee e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id=o.id) SELECT * FROM org;
followups: How do you prevent infinite recursion?
Can recursive CTEs traverse arbitrary graphs?
mistakes: Forgetting cycle handling in cyclic data.
interview: Recursive CTEs are useful for hierarchical traversal, but cyclic data requires explicit safeguards or visited-state logic.

title: What is keyset pagination and why is it often better than OFFSET?
short: Keyset pagination uses a stable ordering key from the last page instead of skipping N rows with OFFSET.
answer: OFFSET can become expensive as the page number grows because the database may scan and discard many rows. Keyset pagination uses a predicate such as created_at/id > lastSeen and an appropriate index.
code: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE (created_at,id) < (?,?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50;
followups: How do you handle non-unique sort keys?
mistakes: Using only created_at when timestamps can tie.
interview: Keyset pagination scales better for deep pages when the ordering columns are indexed and stable. I use a tie-breaker such as the primary key.

title: What is a database deadlock?
short: A deadlock occurs when transactions hold resources while waiting for each other, creating a cycle.
answer: For example, transaction A locks row 1 then waits for row 2 while transaction B locks row 2 then waits for row 1. Databases detect deadlocks and abort one transaction.
code:
T1: lock A -> wait B
T2: lock B -> wait A
followups: Why should applications retry deadlock victims?
mistakes: Assuming increasing the transaction timeout fixes the cycle.
interview: Deadlocks are cyclic waits. Consistent lock ordering, short transactions and appropriate indexes reduce them, while applications should safely retry transactions chosen as victims.

title: How can you reduce SQL deadlocks?
short: Reduce lock duration, access rows in a consistent order and avoid unnecessary work inside transactions.
answer: Good indexes reduce the rows locked or scanned. Consistent ordering prevents cycles, and smaller transactions reduce contention. Deadlock retry should be bounded and idempotent.
code: Always update rows in ascending ID order
followups: Can SELECT queries participate in locking?
Why do missing indexes increase contention?
mistakes: Adding random retries without fixing the lock order.
interview: I reduce deadlocks through consistent access order, proper indexes, short transaction scope and safe retry of aborted transactions.

title: What is optimistic locking in JPA/SQL?
short: Optimistic locking detects concurrent updates using a version column rather than holding a long database lock.
answer: A row includes a version. An update succeeds only if the version still matches the value read. If zero rows are updated, the application detects a conflict and decides whether to retry or report it.
code: UPDATE product SET price=?, version=version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=?;
followups: How is this different from SELECT FOR UPDATE?
What user experience should a conflict produce?
mistakes: Silently overwriting a concurrent update.
interview: Optimistic locking is appropriate when conflicts are relatively rare and long blocking locks are undesirable.

title: What is SELECT FOR UPDATE?
short: SELECT FOR UPDATE reads rows while acquiring locks intended to protect them from conflicting updates until the transaction ends.
answer: It is useful when a transaction must read current state and then update it without another transaction changing the row in between. Lock duration and isolation behavior depend on the database.
code: BEGIN; SELECT balance FROM account WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; UPDATE account SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
followups: What happens if another transaction requests the same lock?
mistakes: Using row locks for read-only queries.
interview: SELECT FOR UPDATE is a pessimistic concurrency tool. It can protect a read-modify-write operation but increases contention if held too long.

title: What is transaction isolation and why does it matter?
short: Isolation controls which concurrent transaction effects a transaction can observe.
answer: Higher isolation can prevent anomalies such as dirty, non-repeatable or phantom reads but may increase locking or coordination. The exact implementation differs by database.
code: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
followups: Explain dirty vs non-repeatable vs phantom read.
Which isolation level does your database default to?
mistakes: Claiming SERIALIZABLE is always the best choice.
interview: Isolation is a correctness/performance trade-off. I choose the lowest level that safely prevents the anomalies relevant to the business operation.

title: What is a dirty read?
short: A dirty read occurs when one transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not committed.
answer: If the writer later rolls back, the reader observed a value that never became committed state. Isolation levels that prevent dirty reads are common in production systems.
code:
T1: UPDATE balance=50 (uncommitted)
T2: SELECT balance -> 50
followups: Which isolation levels allow dirty reads?
How is it different from a non-repeatable read?
mistakes: Calling a stale committed value a dirty read.
interview: A dirty read observes uncommitted data. It is distinct from reading a committed value that later changes.

title: What is a phantom read?
short: A phantom read occurs when repeating a predicate query within a transaction returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or removed matching rows.
answer: It differs from a non-repeatable read, which changes an already-read row. Predicate-level protection or serializable techniques are used when phantoms must be prevented.
code:
T1: SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE amount>100
T2: INSERT amount=200
T1: same SELECT -> different count
mistakes: Confusing phantoms with changed column values in an existing row.
interview: A phantom is a change in the set of rows matching a predicate, often caused by concurrent inserts or deletes.

title: What is normalization and why is it used?
short: Normalization organizes data to reduce unnecessary duplication and update anomalies.
answer: Common normal forms progressively constrain dependencies. Normalization improves consistency and write behavior but can require more joins for read-heavy workloads.
code:
Customer(id, name)
Order(id, customer_id, total)
mistakes: Normalizing every system regardless of workload.
interview: Normalization reduces redundancy and anomalies. I balance it against read performance and reporting requirements rather than treating it as an absolute rule.

title: What is a foreign key and what does it enforce?
short: A foreign key enforces that a child value refers to a valid parent key, subject to the configured actions.
answer: It protects referential integrity and can define ON DELETE or ON UPDATE behavior. Foreign keys also influence delete/update costs and indexing choices.
code: FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customer(id)
followups: Should foreign keys always be indexed?
mistakes: Using application checks as the only integrity mechanism.
interview: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity at the database boundary. I still design indexes and cascade behavior carefully for performance and safety.

title: What is a unique constraint vs a unique index?
short: Both can enforce uniqueness, but a constraint expresses a data rule while an index is primarily a physical access structure; exact behavior varies by database.
answer: A UNIQUE constraint often creates or uses a unique index internally. Use constraints to express business invariants and indexes intentionally for access paths.
code: ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_users_email UNIQUE(email);
followups: Can a unique constraint contain NULL?
How do composite unique constraints work?
mistakes: Assuming NULL uniqueness behaves identically in every database.
interview: A unique constraint expresses a uniqueness rule and is typically backed by an index. NULL semantics vary by database, so I verify the target engine.

title: What is a partial or filtered index?
short: A partial index stores entries only for rows matching a predicate, reducing index size and focusing on a common query subset.
answer: For example, an index on active users can exclude inactive rows. Support and syntax depend on the database.
code: CREATE INDEX idx_active_users ON users(email) WHERE active = true;
followups: When is a partial index useful?
Does MySQL support the same syntax?
mistakes: Assuming all database engines implement filtered indexes identically.
interview: A partial index is valuable when queries repeatedly target a selective subset. The exact syntax and optimizer behavior are database-specific.

title: Why can functions on indexed columns hurt index usage?
short: Wrapping an indexed column in a function can prevent the optimizer from using a normal index efficiently, depending on the database.
answer: For example, WHERE LOWER(email)=? may require a functional index or a normalized stored value. Rewriting predicates to preserve sargability can help.
code:
-- Instead of: WHERE DATE(created_at)=?
-- consider a range: created_at >= ? AND created_at < ?
mistakes: Applying functions to indexed columns without checking the plan.
interview: I prefer predicates that allow an index range scan, or I create an appropriate functional index when the database supports it.

title: What is a sargable query?
short: A sargable predicate allows the database to use an index efficiently to locate qualifying rows.
answer: Range and equality predicates on indexed columns are common examples. Wrapping columns in functions or leading wildcard patterns can reduce index usefulness.
code: WHERE created_at >= ? AND created_at < ?
followups: How do expressions affect index usage?
mistakes: Equating any indexed column with automatic index use.
interview: Sargability is about writing predicates the optimizer can turn into efficient index access paths.

title: What is a database connection pool and why does pool size matter?
short: A connection pool reuses database connections and limits concurrent database work.
answer: Too few connections can create application-side waiting; too many can overload the database with concurrent work. Pool sizing should consider database capacity, query latency and the number of application instances.
code: maximumPoolSize=20
followups: How do you size the pool across 10 instances?
What does pool exhaustion look like?
mistakes: Setting maximumPoolSize to hundreds on every pod.
interview: Connection pools are both a performance optimization and a concurrency limit. The total pool capacity across instances must fit database capacity.

title: How do you optimize an N+1 query problem in SQL?
short: N+1 occurs when one query loads parent rows and then one additional query runs per parent.
answer: Replace repeated lookups with an appropriate join, batch query or set-based operation. Verify the result cardinality and indexes because an overly broad join can create a different performance problem.
code: SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customer c ON c.id=o.customer_id;
followups: N+1 in JPA vs plain JDBC?
When can a join be worse?
mistakes: Fixing N+1 with an enormous Cartesian join.
interview: I replace row-by-row queries with set-based access such as joins or IN queries, then verify the execution plan and returned row count.

title: Why is SELECT * discouraged in production queries?
short: SELECT * can fetch unnecessary columns, increase network and memory usage, and make contracts unstable when schemas evolve.
answer: Selecting only required columns can reduce I/O and allow covering indexes. It also makes application dependencies explicit.
code: SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id=?;
followups: How can it affect covering indexes?
mistakes: Using SELECT * for large APIs or wide tables by default.
interview: I select only the columns needed by the use case, especially for large or frequently executed queries.

title: How do you troubleshoot a query that suddenly became slow?
short: Start by comparing the execution plan and runtime with the previously healthy state.
answer: Check data growth, statistics, index changes, parameter sensitivity, blocking/locks, schema changes and resource saturation. Capture the exact query and parameters, then test a targeted fix and verify it under representative load.
code: EXPLAIN ANALYZE <query>
followups: What if the plan changed after data growth?
mistakes: Adding an index without identifying the changed behavior.
interview: I compare plans and runtime, then investigate data distribution, statistics, locks, indexes and resource saturation before changing the query.

title: What is query parameterization and why is it important?
short: Parameterized queries separate SQL structure from user-supplied values and help prevent SQL injection.
answer: The database driver binds values rather than concatenating them into SQL text. Parameterization also improves statement reuse in many systems.
code:
PreparedStatement ps=conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email=?");
ps.setString(1,email);
mistakes: Building SQL by string concatenation with user input.
interview: I use parameterized queries for values. Dynamic identifiers require a strict allowlist because they cannot usually be bound as ordinary parameters.

title: What is SQL injection?
short: SQL injection occurs when untrusted input changes the structure of a SQL statement.
answer: Concatenating user input into SQL can let an attacker alter predicates or execute unintended commands. Parameterized queries, least privilege and validation reduce the risk.
code:
BAD: "SELECT ... WHERE name= + input + "
GOOD: PreparedStatement
followups: Can stored procedures prevent injection automatically?
mistakes: Relying only on escaping strings.
interview: SQL injection is prevented primarily by separating SQL code from data using parameterized queries and by limiting database privileges.

title: How do indexes affect INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE performance?
short: Indexes speed reads but add maintenance work to writes because affected index entries must also be updated.
answer: A table with many indexes can make high-write workloads slower and increase storage. Indexes should be justified by important access patterns and monitored for usefulness.
code: INSERT order -> update primary/index entries
followups: How do you identify unused indexes?
mistakes: Adding an index for every query without considering writes.
interview: Indexes are a trade-off: faster reads versus additional write, storage and maintenance cost.

title: What is partitioning in a database?
short: Partitioning splits a logical table into smaller physical partitions based on a key such as date or tenant.
answer: Partition pruning can reduce the amount of data scanned. Partitioning can also help maintenance and archival, but it does not automatically fix poorly designed queries.
code: PARTITION BY RANGE(created_at)
followups: How do you choose a partition key?
mistakes: Assuming partitioning makes every query faster.
interview: Partitioning organizes one logical table into manageable pieces. It is useful when queries align with the partition key and data lifecycle.

title: Partitioning vs sharding
short: Partitioning divides data within a database system; sharding distributes data across separate database nodes or clusters.
answer: Partitioning can simplify pruning and maintenance within a database. Sharding adds horizontal capacity but requires routing, cross-shard query strategy and operational complexity.
code:
Partitioning: one cluster
Sharding: shard A/B/C
followups: How do you choose a shard key?
mistakes: Using sharding before exhausting simpler scaling options.
interview: Partitioning is often a database-local organization technique; sharding distributes ownership across nodes. Sharding should be driven by capacity and access-pattern requirements.

title: How do you read an execution plan for a slow query?
short: Find expensive operators, poor access paths and row-estimate errors, then compare actual behavior with the expected plan.
answer: Look for large scans, bad join strategies, repeated loops, sorts/spills and cardinality misestimation. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE where supported and verify indexes/statistics.
code: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ...;
followups: When can a full scan be correct?
mistakes: Adding indexes without reading the plan.
interview: I identify the most expensive operator and validate why the optimizer chose it before changing indexes or SQL.

title: How do you choose composite index column order?
short: Match leading index columns to real equality, range and ordering predicates.
answer: Composite B-tree indexes are ordered by leading columns. A common pattern is equality predicates followed by range/order columns, but workload and plan evidence decide the final order.
code: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status_created ON orders(customer_id,status,created_at);
mistakes: Always putting the highest-cardinality column first.
interview: I choose index order from query patterns, not a universal selectivity rule, then verify with the execution plan.

title: How do you prevent and recover from database deadlocks?
short: Use consistent lock ordering, short transactions and appropriate indexes; retry the whole transaction when a deadlock victim is detected.
answer: Different update orders create cycles. Consistent ordering and reduced transaction scope lower probability. Recovery must repeat the logical transaction because the database may have rolled it back.
code: UPDATE accounts SET ... WHERE id IN (?,?) ORDER BY id;
mistakes: Retrying only one SQL statement inside a rolled-back transaction.
interview: Deadlocks are a concurrency condition. I reduce them by design and make safe retries part of the application behavior.

title: When is keyset pagination better than OFFSET?
short: Keyset pagination scales better for deep pages because it seeks from the last seen key instead of skipping many rows.
answer: Use a deterministic composite ordering such as created_at plus id and query from the last tuple. It is ideal for feeds/infinite scroll but less convenient for arbitrary page numbers.
code: WHERE (created_at,id) < (?,?) ORDER BY created_at DESC,id DESC LIMIT 50
followups: How do you make ordering deterministic?
mistakes: Using a non-unique sort key alone.
interview: For large tables I prefer keyset pagination when users move sequentially through results.

title: How do you diagnose connection-pool exhaustion?
short: Inspect pool waiters, connection hold time, slow queries and database capacity before increasing pool size.
answer: A full pool can come from leaks, long transactions, slow queries or an undersized pool. Increasing it blindly can simply overload the database.
code: metrics: active, idle, pending, acquireLatency, usageDuration
followups: How do you choose pool size?
mistakes: Increasing max connections until the DB saturates.
interview: I correlate pool metrics with SQL and transaction traces to identify why connections are held too long.

title: How do window functions differ from GROUP BY?
short: GROUP BY collapses rows; window functions calculate across related rows while retaining row detail.
answer: Use ROW_NUMBER/RANK for ranking, LAG/LEAD for comparisons and SUM OVER for running totals.
code: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC)
mistakes: Using GROUP BY and losing row-level detail.
interview: I use GROUP BY for one row per group and window functions when I need group calculations alongside each original row.

title: How do you archive a huge table safely?
short: Move cold data in controlled batches or partitions and avoid giant delete transactions.
answer: Time-based partitioning can make retention a metadata operation. Otherwise archive by stable key in bounded batches while monitoring locks, WAL/redo and replication lag.
code: -- Prefer partition detach/drop for time-based retention.
mistakes: One huge DELETE during peak traffic.
interview: For very large historical data I prefer partition-based retention because dropping an old partition is safer than deleting millions of rows in one transaction.

title: How do you design an idempotent database command?
short: Use a unique business/idempotency key and atomic insert/update semantics.
answer: A unique constraint works across instances and restarts. Handle duplicate-key outcomes by returning or loading the existing logical result.
code: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_payment_key ON payments(idempotency_key);
followups: How do you return the original response?
How do you handle concurrent requests?
mistakes: Check-then-insert in separate non-atomic steps.
interview: Database uniqueness is a strong primitive for idempotency because the database arbitrates concurrent first attempts.

title: How do you perform a large data backfill safely?
short: Use small batches, stable keys, throttling and observability so the backfill does not starve production traffic.
answer: Prefer primary-key ranges, commit frequently, pause on replication lag or lock pressure, and make the job restartable.
code: UPDATE users SET new_col=... WHERE id > ? AND id <= ?;
mistakes: One massive transaction for millions of rows.
interview: A backfill is production workload. I make it resumable, bounded and adaptive to database health.

title: How do you diagnose lock contention?
short: Find blocked sessions, lock owners, transaction age and the SQL holding the resource.
answer: Long transactions and missing indexes often turn small updates into long lock waits. Correlate database lock views with application traces and transaction boundaries.
code: -- Inspect blocked/blocked-by sessions using DB-specific lock views.
mistakes: Only increasing timeout values.
interview: I identify who is waiting, who holds the lock and why the holder is slow. Then I shorten the transaction or improve the access path.

title: A query becomes slow after the table grows tenfold
short: Query performance is data-dependent; an index that worked at small scale may become ineffective as selectivity and distribution change.
answer: I would compare execution plans and cardinality estimates first. Then I would tune indexes or query shape, update statistics and consider partitioning or archival only if the data model and access pattern justify it.
code: Choose indexes based on the actual predicates and ordering, update statistics and reduce unnecessary rows/columns. If the workload has outgrown one table, consider partitioning or archival based on access patterns.
followups: When can an optimizer ignore an index?
mistakes: Adding indexes without checking write cost.
Optimizing only against a tiny test dataset.
interview: I would not tune SQL from the text alone. I need the execution plan and realistic data distribution.
scenario: A query that was fast with 2 million rows becomes slow at 20 million rows even though the SQL text has not changed.
investigation: Compare execution plans before and after growth. Inspect row estimates, index usage, scan type, selectivity, sort/hash operations and returned row counts.
resolution: Choose indexes based on the actual predicates and ordering, update statistics and reduce unnecessary rows/columns. If the workload has outgrown one table, consider partitioning or archival based on access patterns.
prevention: Monitor plan regressions, index usage and data growth. Include representative data volume in performance testing.

title: A deadlock appears after a new transaction flow is deployed
short: Deadlocks usually come from inconsistent lock ordering combined with concurrency.
answer: I would inspect the deadlock graph, identify the lock order and make the transaction paths acquire resources consistently. I would also keep transactions short and use bounded retry only when the business operation is safe to repeat.
code: Make transactions acquire shared resources in a consistent order, keep transactions short and avoid unnecessary locks. Add safe retry for deadlock victims when the operation is idempotent and the database recommends it.
followups: How do isolation levels affect locking?
mistakes: Increasing lock timeouts.
Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly.
interview: I would fix the lock-ordering design first and use retry only as a resilience measure, not the primary solution.
scenario: Two transactions update the same business entities in different orders. Under concurrency, each waits for a lock held by the other.
investigation: Capture deadlock graphs or database diagnostics. Identify the resources and lock acquisition order for each transaction.
resolution: Make transactions acquire shared resources in a consistent order, keep transactions short and avoid unnecessary locks. Add safe retry for deadlock victims when the operation is idempotent and the database recommends it.
prevention: Test concurrent access patterns, monitor deadlock frequency and document lock ordering for critical workflows.

title: An index exists but the query still performs a full scan
short: Having an index is not enough; the predicate must allow the optimizer to use it efficiently.
answer: I would inspect the plan and predicate. If a function wraps the indexed column, I would usually rewrite it as a range predicate so the database can use the index, then verify with EXPLAIN.
code: Rewrite predicates into sargable ranges where possible, for example a half-open timestamp interval. Use functional indexes only when supported and justified by workload.
followups: When is a functional index useful?
Why can a selective index still be ignored?
mistakes: Assuming every WHERE clause can use the index.
Applying functions to indexed columns unnecessarily.
interview: I would validate index usability through the execution plan, not by checking that the index exists.
scenario: A query filters on a timestamp column with a function applied to it. An index exists, but the optimizer chooses a full table scan.
investigation: Inspect the predicate and execution plan. Check whether the expression prevents efficient index range access and whether selectivity is sufficient.
resolution: Rewrite predicates into sargable ranges where possible, for example a half-open timestamp interval. Use functional indexes only when supported and justified by workload.
prevention: Review common predicates during index design and test with production-like statistics.

title: A large delete locks the table and causes API timeouts
short: Large maintenance transactions can create operational incidents even when the SQL is logically correct.
answer: I would avoid one giant transaction. I would batch the deletion, control commit frequency and consider partition-based retention if the data is naturally time-partitioned.
code: Delete in bounded batches, commit between batches when business rules allow and schedule heavy maintenance during lower traffic. For very large time-based data, partitioning can make retention operations cheaper.
followups: When should batching not be used?
How does partition dropping help retention?
What are the consistency implications of batch deletes?
mistakes: Deleting millions of rows in one transaction.
Ignoring transaction-log and replication impact.
interview: For large data operations I care about lock duration, log volume and impact on foreground traffic, not only total execution time.
scenario: A maintenance job deletes millions of old rows in one transaction. Application requests start timing out because of lock and I/O pressure.
investigation: Inspect transaction duration, lock waits, log growth and database I/O. Determine whether the delete conflicts with active queries.
resolution: Delete in bounded batches, commit between batches when business rules allow and schedule heavy maintenance during lower traffic. For very large time-based data, partitioning can make retention operations cheaper.
prevention: Load-test maintenance jobs against production-like traffic and monitor lock duration and transaction log growth.

title: Pagination becomes slower on deep pages
short: OFFSET pagination makes the database walk past rows that are not returned; keyset pagination starts from the last seen key.
answer: For very deep pages I would replace OFFSET with keyset pagination using an indexed, deterministic sort key such as created_at plus a unique ID. This keeps work closer to the requested page size.
code: Use keyset/seek pagination based on a stable indexed ordering for large datasets. Keep cursor semantics explicit and avoid exposing mutable offset-based navigation when consistent traversal matters.
followups: How do you paginate with duplicate timestamps?
mistakes: Using only created_at when timestamps are not unique.
Treating a cursor as a random page number.
interview: I would use offset pagination for simple shallow navigation and keyset pagination for large, high-volume feeds.
scenario: An API uses OFFSET 5,000,000 LIMIT 50. The first pages are fast, but deep pages become increasingly slow.
investigation: Inspect the execution plan and amount of rows scanned/discarded before the requested page. Measure latency as offset grows.
resolution: Use keyset/seek pagination based on a stable indexed ordering for large datasets. Keep cursor semantics explicit and avoid exposing mutable offset-based navigation when consistent traversal matters.
prevention: Index the cursor columns, define deterministic ordering and test pagination at realistic data volume.

title: SQL query becomes slow after table growth
short: A query can degrade as data volume grows because an old plan or index strategy no longer matches the data distribution.
answer: I would not immediately add an index. I would inspect the execution plan and identify whether the database is scanning too many rows, sorting, or using a poor join strategy. Then I would change the query or index based on evidence and measure again.
followups: When can an index make writes slower?
mistakes: Do not index every column.
interview: The interview answer should emphasize execution plans and selectivity rather than saying indexes always make queries faster.
scenario: A query that used to run in 50 ms now takes 8 seconds after a table grows from one million to fifty million rows.
investigation: Capture the execution plan, inspect row estimates, index usage, selectivity, sort/hash operations and whether predicates are sargable. Compare the plan before and after growth if possible.
prevention: Design indexes based on actual predicates and ordering, rewrite non-sargable expressions, update statistics where applicable, reduce unnecessary columns and consider partitioning only when it solves a demonstrated access pattern.

title: Two services deadlock while updating shared business data
short: Deadlocks happen when transactions hold locks while waiting for each other in a cycle.
answer: I would confirm the cycle in the database deadlock report. The primary fix is to acquire shared resources in a consistent order across code paths. Retries can be a secondary resilience mechanism, but they should not hide a systemic locking problem.
followups: How is a deadlock different from lock timeout?
What isolation level changes might help?
mistakes: Do not rely only on retries.
interview: Consistent lock ordering is often the simplest preventive design.
scenario: Service A updates order then inventory. Service B updates inventory then order. Under concurrency, requests start deadlocking.
investigation: Inspect database deadlock reports and transaction traces to identify lock acquisition order. Confirm whether both operations touch the same rows in opposite order.
prevention: Standardize lock acquisition order, keep transactions short, avoid unnecessary locks, and implement bounded retry for transient deadlock failures.

title: Offset pagination becomes extremely slow on a large table
short: Offset pagination can become expensive at deep pages because the database still processes skipped rows.
answer: For large datasets I would prefer keyset pagination. The client sends the last seen key, and the database can use an index to seek directly into the next range. This gives more stable performance as the page depth increases.
followups: How do you paginate by timestamp safely?
mistakes: Do not claim keyset always works for arbitrary sorting without a stable unique tie-breaker.
interview: The trade-off is that keyset pagination is less convenient for random page-number navigation.
scenario: Page 1 of an API is fast, but requesting page 50,000 takes several seconds.
investigation: Inspect the SQL and execution plan. OFFSET often requires the database to walk past a large number of rows before returning the requested page.
prevention: Use keyset/seek pagination with a stable indexed ordering, such as WHERE id > lastSeenId ORDER BY id LIMIT n. Document that arbitrary page-number jumps may no longer be supported.

title: A SQL query causes lock contention during a batch job
short: Long-running batch transactions can create lock contention even when the individual SQL statements are fast.
answer: I would reduce transaction scope and batch size first, then inspect lock waits and the access plan. The batch should acquire locks predictably and release them frequently enough that interactive traffic can make progress.
followups: How would you throttle a backfill?
mistakes: Do not solve lock contention only by increasing database resources.
interview: The best batch size is workload-specific; measure lock duration and throughput rather than picking a huge fixed number.
scenario: A nightly batch update causes daytime API requests to wait on locked rows.
investigation: Inspect transaction duration, lock wait events, batch size and whether the batch scans or updates rows in a conflicting order.
prevention: Break work into smaller committed batches, process in deterministic key order, use appropriate indexes, schedule heavy work carefully and avoid holding locks while doing unrelated work.

title: What is a partial index and when is it useful?
short: A partial or filtered index indexes only rows satisfying a predicate.
answer: It can reduce index size and improve targeted queries when a stable subset is frequently accessed, such as active records. Support and syntax vary by database.
followups: What happens when the predicate changes?
interview: A partial index is useful when a query repeatedly targets a subset of rows. I verify that the optimizer can use it and that the predicate matches the workload.

title: What is an index-only scan?
short: An index-only scan can satisfy a query using index data without visiting the base table when visibility and required columns permit.
answer: It can reduce I/O, especially for covering indexes, but maintenance cost and visibility rules still matter.
followups: How is it different from a covering index?
interview: Index-only access can be very fast for read-heavy queries, but I balance wider indexes against write and storage overhead.

title: How do foreign keys affect performance?
short: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity but can add work to inserts, updates and deletes.
answer: Referenced and referencing columns should be indexed appropriately for common operations. Constraints are usually worth the correctness they provide, but large cascades need careful design.
interview: Foreign keys protect correctness. I index the referencing columns when needed and pay attention to cascade behavior on large tables.

title: What is a database connection leak?
short: A connection leak occurs when application code fails to return a borrowed connection to the pool.
answer: Over time active connections reach the pool maximum and requests wait or fail. Proper resource management, pool leak detection and metrics help diagnose it.
followups: Why does traffic make the issue worse?
interview: I correlate pool active count and pending acquisition with code paths. In JDBC, try-with-resources and framework-managed transactions prevent many leaks.

title: What is MVCC?
short: Multi-version concurrency control lets readers and writers operate using versions of rows rather than blocking each other in the simplest cases.
answer: Different databases implement MVCC differently. It improves read/write concurrency but creates version cleanup and isolation considerations.
interview: MVCC maintains multiple row versions so readers can see a consistent snapshot while writers proceed. Exact semantics depend on the database.

title: How do database locks escalate?
short: Some database systems can replace many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock to reduce lock-management overhead.
answer: Escalation can increase contention and cause unexpected blocking during large operations. Batching and appropriate indexes can reduce the number of locked rows.
interview: Lock escalation is a database-specific behavior where many locks can become a larger lock. Large batch operations should be designed with this possibility in mind.
scenario: Some database systems can replace many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock to reduce lock-management overhead.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is parameterized SQL and why does it matter?
short: Parameterized SQL separates SQL structure from user-supplied values.
answer: Prepared statements prevent input from being interpreted as SQL syntax and can also improve plan reuse depending on the database.
interview: I always bind user values through prepared statements or framework parameters. String concatenation is both unsafe and harder to maintain.

title: How do you implement an idempotent database command?
short: An idempotent command produces the same final state when safely repeated.
answer: Use unique business keys, upserts, compare-and-set updates or state checks. The database constraint should enforce uniqueness where correctness depends on it.
followups: How do you handle duplicate requests?
interview: I prefer database-enforced uniqueness and conditional state transitions over relying only on application checks.

title: What is a covering query and why can SELECT * be harmful?
short: A query is easier to cover when it selects only the columns it needs.
answer: SELECT * increases network payload, deserialization and the set of columns an index must cover. Schema changes can also unexpectedly change its cost.
followups: Why is it a maintenance risk?
interview: I select only required columns, especially in APIs and hot queries. It keeps payloads smaller and gives indexes a realistic chance to cover the access path.

title: How do you find gaps in sequential IDs?
short: Gaps can be identified by comparing each value with the previous value or expected sequence.
answer: Window functions such as LAG can reveal discontinuities. Whether gaps are a problem depends on the ID generation strategy; auto-increment sequences commonly allow gaps.
followups: Why are auto-increment IDs not gapless?
When do you need a business sequence?
interview: I can detect gaps with LAG or generate an expected sequence, but I don't assume IDs must be gapless because transaction rollback and sequence caching can create gaps.

title: What is a recursive CTE useful for?
short: A recursive CTE queries hierarchical or graph-like relationships such as employee-manager trees.
answer: It has an anchor query and a recursive member and needs termination conditions. Large or cyclic graphs require safeguards.
followups: When would you use application traversal?
interview: Recursive CTEs are useful for hierarchies when the database supports them. I define a clear termination condition and protect against cycles or excessive depth.

title: How do you detect skew in a database workload?
short: Skew means a small subset of keys or queries receives disproportionate traffic or data.
answer: Hot tenants, hot rows and popular products can create contention even when average load looks healthy. Partitioning, caching and sharding strategies must account for skew.
followups: How do hot rows cause contention?
How do you mitigate hot keys?
interview: I look at per-key and per-query distributions, not just averages. A hot key can dominate latency and CPU even when overall utilization seems moderate.
scenario: Skew means a small subset of keys or queries receives disproportionate traffic or data.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is write amplification in databases?
short: Write amplification means the system performs more physical or logical writes than the application-level change suggests.
answer: Indexes, WAL/redo logs, page splits, replication and secondary structures can all add write work. It affects storage, I/O and throughput.
interview: Adding indexes improves reads but increases write amplification because every insert/update may maintain more structures.

title: How do you safely change a primary key type on a large table?
short: Changing a key type on a large table can require coordinated changes to indexes, foreign keys and application code.
answer: Use an expand-and-contract migration: introduce the new key representation, backfill, support both versions, migrate references, validate, then remove the old structure.
followups: How do you backfill without blocking?
interview: I avoid an in-place destructive change. I introduce the new representation compatibly, migrate references incrementally and remove the old key only after all consumers are moved.

title: How do you investigate lock contention without a deadlock?
short: Blocking can occur even without a cycle when one transaction holds a resource for a long time.
answer: Identify the blocking session, SQL statement, transaction age and lock resource. Reduce transaction scope, add indexes, commit sooner or redesign access patterns.
followups: How do you find the blocker?
Can a slow query cause blocking?
interview: A lock wait is not automatically a deadlock. I find the blocker, inspect why its transaction is long, and fix the root cause rather than merely increasing timeouts.
scenario: Blocking can occur even without a cycle when one transaction holds a resource for a long time.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.
